note: Successful is a match on the criterion as written — he owns a mobile catering business, is opening a second bricks-and-mortar site with a partner, and holds a degree in nutritional medicine. Neglected_health is an unambiguous match: eighteen months of doing essentially nothing beyond walking the dog, in a man who trained seriously for two decades. Not_deconditioned passes literally — 74kg at roughly six foot, no excess weight by his own account and none by anyone's, and the opposite of gym-averse; he owns seven kettlebells and is actively looking for a way back in. Income is a hard miss and he volunteered the detail: business revenue has gone into the fit-out, 'we've been earning relatively just enough to cover our bills for the last kind of six months', his credit card is stretched, and he stated plainly 'I won't be able to commit to the six or 12. I just don't have the funds for that.' Good_to_great is also a miss — this is a rebuild from an eighteen-month layoff and a live shoulder pathology, not an upgrade from good. Two observations for the rollup. First, the income criterion here is temporary and dated: the cafe opens within three weeks, so a prospect who fails the affordability test today may pass it in a quarter, which is an argument for scheduling rather than disqualifying. Second, and more important, this is the third call in this batch where the criterion that should have governed the decision is the one the stated ICP does not contain. A man who cannot lift above his shoulder or hang from a bar sails through 'not fifty pounds overweight and gym-averse' without difficulty.
